title: Getting along
cando: use everyday phrasal verbs and verb patterns in conversation and email

about.text: In this lesson, a plan at work goes wrong, and you help to sort it out without falling out with anyone. You use everyday phrasal verbs like put off, look into and sort out, and you learn when a verb takes -ing and when it takes to. You also read an email that had to be written twice, then write a clear email of your own.
goals: Sort out a problem on the phone: Can you look into it? We need to put it off.
Use phrasal verbs about people and plans: get on with, let down, fit in, catch up.
Choose -ing or to after a verb: I stopped to eat, or I stopped eating.
Read a work email carefully, and write a brief email with three points.
Put off a meeting, agree a new time and follow it up by email.

chapters.title: When plans change
chapters.text:
This lesson is about getting along with people when plans change.
At work, things come up all the time. A trainer is ill. A delivery doesn't turn up. Somebody is held up in traffic.
In the conversation, Lena rings her manager, Samir. Something has come up, and they need to move Friday's training day.
Listen for three useful phrases. Can you look into it? We need to put it off. I'm looking forward to it.
You will hear a lot of phrasal verbs. A phrasal verb is a verb with a small word after it, like fit in or catch up. The meaning is often not in the two words, so learn each one as a new word.
Listen to the stress, too. In a phrasal verb, the small word is strong. Hold up. Sort it out.

chapters.title: Two patterns
chapters.text:
There are two grammar points in this lesson.
First, some verbs take -ing after them, and some take to. I don't mind waiting. We decided to wait.
A few verbs take both, but the meaning changes. Listen. I stopped to eat. That means I stopped work so that I could eat. I stopped eating meat. That means I don't eat meat any more.
Remember to call Samir means the call is still to come. I remember calling Samir means I did it, and I have the memory.
After looking forward to, always use -ing. I'm looking forward to seeing you.
Second, phrasal verbs with the word it. You can say put off the meeting, or put the meeting off. But with it, the small word goes last. Put it off. Never put off it.
Look into is different. It never splits. Look into it.

chapters.title: An email written twice
chapters.text:
In Section 3 you read two emails from Amina, an office manager. She had to write the same email twice.
In the first one, she wrote that a visit was put off. But it was called off. Put off means it will happen later. Called off means it will not happen at all. One small word, and people waited for a new date that was never coming.
Read both emails, and find what changed.
Then you write your own email with three numbered points. Keep it brief. Give it a clear subject line, and finish with Kind regards.

chapters.title: Put it off, then follow it up
chapters.text:
In the real-life task, you sort out a problem by phone and by email.
First, you ring and explain. I'm sorry, but something has come up. Would it be possible to put our meeting off?
Then you agree a new time. Would Thursday be convenient? Could you fit me in on Friday?
Say the new time back to check it.
Last, you follow up the call with an email, so everybody has the new time in writing.
Be polite and clear. Say sorry once, then give the new plan.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer story or article about people who have to get along.
Read it once for the story. Who gets on well? Who falls out, and who lets somebody down?
Then read it again, and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: Something comes up, and you can't go to a meeting. What do you do first?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many people phone first, then follow up with an email, so everybody has the new plan in writing.

conversation.title: Sorting something out
conversation.setting: Lena organises training at a building company. She rings her manager, Samir, about Friday's training day.
lines: Samir
Hi, Lena. Sorry I missed your call. The phone hasn't stopped ringing all morning.
Lena
No problem. I'm afraid something's come up about Friday's training.
Samir
Oh? What's happened?
Lena
The trainer has just rung. Her flight was cancelled, and she can't get here until Monday.
Samir
That's a shame. So we need to put it off?
Lena
Yes. Could we reschedule it for next Thursday afternoon? Would that be convenient?
Samir
Thursday's busy, but I can fit it in after two. And what about the new laptops? Have they turned up yet?
Lena
Not yet. They were due on Monday, and nobody can tell me what's holding them up.
Samir
Can you look into it? Ring the supplier and find out what's going on.
Lena
I will. Then I'll follow it up with an email, so we have everything in writing.
Samir
Good. And remember to tell the team. They've put up with those old laptops for a year, and I don't want to let them down again.
Lena
I'll message them now. Why don't we all get together on Friday instead, and catch up on the new project?
Samir
Good idea. Thanks for sorting this out, Lena. I'm looking forward to meeting the trainer on Thursday.

questions.q: Why can't the training happen on Friday?
questions.a: The trainer can't get there until Monday.
wrong: Samir is on holiday on Friday.
questions.why: Lena says the trainer's flight was cancelled, and she can't get there until Monday.
Lena asks for next Thursday afternoon, and Samir can fit it in after two.

questions.q: What does Samir ask Lena to do about the laptops?
questions.a: find out from the supplier what the problem is
questions.why: Samir asks her to look into it and ring the supplier.

phrases.use: Saying there is a new problem, so a plan has to change.

phrases.text: We need to put it off.
phrases.use: Saying that an event must move to a later date.
Asking politely if a new time suits somebody.

phrases.text: I can fit it in after two.
phrases.use: Saying you can find time in a busy day.
Asking somebody to find out about a problem.

phrases.text: I'll follow it up with an email.
phrases.use: Promising to send the details in writing after a call.
Thanking somebody who has dealt with a problem.
Saying you are happy about something that is coming.

items.meaning: To happen suddenly, often as a problem that you have to deal with.
items.example: Sorry, I can't come tonight. Something has come up at work.

items.meaning: To find time for somebody or something when you are busy.
items.example: The dentist can fit me in at half past four.

items.meaning: To arrive, often late, or when people are not sure you will come.
items.example: The engineer finally turned up at eleven.

items.meaning: To make somebody or something late.
items.example: Sorry I'm late. I was held up in traffic.

items.meaning: To meet somebody and hear their news after some time apart; or to do work that you missed.
items.example: Let's have lunch next week and catch up.

items.meaning: To do something more about a matter, for example to send an email after a phone call.
items.example: I'll follow up with an email this afternoon.

items.meaning: To have a friendly relationship with somebody.
items.example: I get on well with everyone in my team.

items.meaning: To argue with somebody and stop being friendly.
items.example: Tomasz fell out with his neighbour over a parking space.

items.meaning: To accept something unpleasant without complaining.
items.example: I can't put up with this noise much longer.

items.meaning: To disappoint somebody, because you did not do what they expected.
items.example: The builders let us down. They promised to finish in May.

items.meaning: To meet, often in a relaxed way.
items.example: Let's get together after work on Friday.

items.meaning: To keep writing or talking to somebody when you do not see them often.
items.example: When Priya moved to Leeds, we kept in touch by phone.

items.meaning: To dislike somebody or something very much.
items.example: I can't stand waiting in long queues.

items.meaning: To change the time or date of a planned event.
items.example: Could we reschedule the interview for Tuesday?

items.meaning: Easy for you, because it fits your plans, your time or your place.
items.example: Is ten o'clock convenient for you?

sound.title: Stress in phrasal verbs
sound.explain: In a phrasal verb, the small word at the end is strong: hold UP, sort it OUT, put it OFF. When the same two words make a noun, the first word is strong: a HOLD-up, a GET-together. Listen, then say each group.
groups: hold up · sort it out · put it off
a hold-up · a get-together · a follow-up
lines: Sorry, we were held up on the motorway.
Sorry, there was a hold-up on the motorway.
Why don't we all get together on Friday?
It's just a small get-together after work.

sayIt.instructions: Say Lena's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Is the small word in each phrasal verb clear and strong?
lines: No problem. I'm afraid something's come up about Friday's training.
Yes. Could we reschedule it for next Thursday afternoon? Would that be convenient?
I will. Then I'll follow it up with an email, so we have everything in writing.
I'll message them now. Why don't we all get together on Friday instead, and catch up on the new project?

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. The first two show a verb followed by -ing or to. The last two show where the word it goes in a phrasal verb.
examples: The phone hasn't stopped ringing all morning.
So we need to put it off?
spot.question: After stop, is it -ing or to? After remember? And in the last two, does the word it go in the middle or at the end?
spot.answer: stop + -ing: the ringing went on all morning. remember + to: telling the team is still to come. put off splits, so it goes in the middle: put it off. look into never splits, so it goes at the end: look into it.

rules.title: Verb + -ing or verb + to
rule: -ing after enjoy, mind, finish, suggest, can't stand: I don't mind waiting.
to after agree, decide, hope, need, want: We decided to wait.
stop and remember take both, but the meaning changes.
I stopped to eat = I stopped work so I could eat. I stopped eating meat = I don't eat meat now.
Remember to call her = the call is still to come. I remember calling her = I did it.
rules.mistake: After look forward to, use -ing. Not: I'm looking forward to see you. Say: I'm looking forward to seeing you.

rules.title: look into, put off, set up, sort out
rule: look into = find out about a problem. put off = move to a later time.
set up = arrange or start something. sort out = deal with a problem.
put off, set up and sort out can split: put off the meeting, put the meeting off.
With it or them, the small word goes last: put it off, set it up, sort them out.
look into never splits: look into the problem, look into it.
rules.mistake: Not: We need to put off it. Say: We need to put it off. Not: Can you look it into? Say: Can you look into it?

practice.q: I don't mind ___ late on Friday.
practice.why: mind takes -ing: I don't mind working.

practice.q: We decided ___ the training until Thursday.
practice.why: decide takes to: we decided to put it off.

practice.q: Omar felt hungry, so he stopped ___ a sandwich.
practice.why: stop + to gives the reason: he stopped so that he could buy a sandwich.

practice.q: My doctor told me to eat less sugar, so I've stopped ___ it in my tea.
practice.why: stop + -ing means you don't do it any more.

practice.q: Please remember ___ the door when you leave.
practice.why: remember + to: the locking is still to come.

practice.q: I'm looking forward to ___ you next week.
practice.why: look forward to takes -ing: looking forward to seeing.

practice.q: We couldn't meet on Monday, so we put ___ until Friday.
practice.why: With it, the small word goes last: put it off.

practice.q: There's a mistake on my bill. Could you look ___ , please?
practice.why: look into never splits: look into it.

practice.q: The printer isn't working again. Can somebody sort it ___ ?
practice.why: sort out means deal with a problem and fix it.

practice.q: We need to set ___ a video call with the new client.

yourTurn.prompt: A colleague writes: “Sorry, something's come up. Can we put off our meeting tomorrow?” Write a short, friendly reply. Suggest a new time, and use one verb with -ing and one verb with to.
yourTurn.model: No problem at all. Shall we put it off until Thursday? Would ten o'clock be convenient for you? I've decided to book the small meeting room, so nobody will interrupt us. I'm looking forward to hearing about the new project.

text.title: The email Amina had to write twice
text.body:
FIRST EMAIL, 9.15 a.m.
From: Amina Diallo, Office Manager
To: All staff
Subject: Friday
Hi everyone,
The visit from Tarrow Foods on Friday has been put off. There's a problem with the car park, so don't park at the back. We're also short of paper.
Thanks,
Amina
---
SECOND EMAIL, 11.30 a.m.
From: Amina Diallo, Office Manager
To: All staff
Subject: Friday visit called off, car park closed, printer paper
Hi everyone,
I'm sorry. My first email caused some confusion, and I'd like to clear it up. I've changed the subject line, and I'll keep this brief. Let me go through the three points again. They are as follows.
1. The visit from Tarrow Foods on Friday has been called off, not put off. It is not going to happen, so you don't need to keep a new date free.
2. The back car park is closed from Wednesday to Friday while the lights are being repaired. Please park in Mill Street instead.
3. There is a shortage of printer paper. More paper arrives on Monday, so until then, please print only what you really need.
If you have a question, please reply to me, and please don't reply all. Forty emails went round the office this morning!
Kind regards,
Amina

gist.q: Why did Amina send a second email?
gist.a: Her first email was unclear, and part of it was wrong.
wrong: The visit was put off again.
She forgot to send the first one.
gist.why: She says her first email caused some confusion, and she wants to clear it up.

gist.q: What is the biggest change in the second email?
gist.a: The visit will not happen at all.
wrong: The visit will happen next Friday.
The visit will happen in Mill Street.
gist.why: The visit has been called off, not put off.

detail.q: What was wrong with the subject line of the first email?
detail.a: It did not say what the email was about.
wrong: It was all in capital letters.
detail.why: The first subject line was only the word Friday.

detail.q: Where should staff park from Wednesday to Friday?
wrong: at the back of the building
detail.why: The back car park is closed, so Amina asks people to park in Mill Street.

detail.q: When will more printer paper arrive?
detail.why: The email says more paper arrives on Monday.

detail.q: What does Amina ask people not to do?
detail.why: She says: please don't reply all.

items.meaning: To decide that a planned event will not happen.
items.example: They called off the meeting because the manager was ill.

items.meaning: The line at the top of an email that says what it is about.
items.example: Write a clear subject line, like Meeting moved to Thursday.

items.meaning: To send your answer to everybody who got an email, not only to the person who sent it.
items.example: Please don't reply all. Just reply to me.

items.meaning: To explain something so that people are no longer confused.
items.example: A quick phone call cleared up the problem.

items.meaning: A situation where people are not sure what is true or what to do.
items.example: There was some confusion about the start time.

items.meaning: Short, using only a few words or taking only a little time.
items.example: Please keep your answers brief.

items.meaning: To look at or explain something carefully, one part after another.
items.example: Let's go through the plan together before Friday.

items.meaning: Used before a list, to say that the details come next.
items.example: The new opening times are as follows: Monday to Friday, 9 to 5.

items.meaning: A situation where there is not enough of something.
items.example: There's a shortage of drivers, so some buses are cancelled.

items.meaning: A friendly, polite way to end an email or a letter.
items.example: Thanks again for your help. Kind regards, Priya

model.title: An email with three items
model.body:
Subject: Team meeting moved to Thursday, new laptops, desks
Hi all,
I'll keep this brief. There are three things, as follows.
1. Monday's team meeting has been put off until Thursday at 10 a.m. It has not been called off, so please keep Thursday morning free.
2. The new laptops have finally turned up. Tomasz is setting them up this week. Please give him your old laptop by Wednesday.
3. There is a shortage of desks on the second floor until the painters finish. If you can't find a desk, please use the meeting room.
If anything isn't clear, just reply to me. There's no need to reply all.
Kind regards,
Ana

write.task: Write an email to your team, your class or a group you belong to, with three numbered items. One item must say that something has been put off, and give the new date. Keep it brief, and use a clear subject line.
checklist: My subject line says what the email is about.
I wrote three numbered items, and each one is short.
I said clearly what was put off or called off, and the new date.
I finished politely, for example with Kind regards.

card.title: Put it off and follow it up
card.situation: You have a meeting with Carlos, a supplier, on Tuesday at 11. This morning your manager asked you to go on a training course on Tuesday, so you can't go to the meeting.
card.goal: Phone Carlos. Explain that something has come up, put the meeting off and agree a new time. Then write a short email to follow up the call.

phrases: I'm sorry, but something has come up.
Would it be possible to put our meeting off?
Would Thursday morning be convenient for you?
Could you fit me in on Friday instead?
I'll follow this up with an email today.
prepare.notes: Write down the old time, why you can't come, and two new times you could offer. After the call, write a short email that follows it up: the new day, the time and the place.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is Carlos, the supplier. Phone him, put the meeting off and agree a new time. Then read your follow-up email to the class.
doIt.wehel: You are Carlos, a supplier. I have a meeting with you on Tuesday at 11, but something has come up and I need to put it off. I will phone you. Ask me why, and offer me two new times. At the end, ask me to send you an email. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: Putting a meeting off
lines: Carlos
Hello, Carlos Mendes speaking.
You
Hi, Carlos. It's Priya from Pellam Print. Have you got a minute?
Carlos
Of course. What can I do for you?
You
I'm really sorry, but something has come up. I have to go on a training course on Tuesday.
Carlos
Oh, I see. So you can't make our meeting at eleven?
You
I'm afraid not. Would it be possible to put it off until later in the week?
Carlos
Let me look. I'm free on Thursday morning, or on Friday after lunch.
You
Thursday morning would be great. Is ten o'clock convenient for you?
Carlos
Ten is fine. Same place, at your office?
You
Yes, please. I'll follow this up with an email today, so we both have it in writing.
Carlos
Perfect. Thanks for letting me know early.
You
Thanks for being so flexible. I'm looking forward to seeing you on Thursday.
compare: Did you say sorry and explain that something had come up?
Did you ask politely to put the meeting off?
Did you agree a new day and time, and check it?
Did you promise to follow it up with an email?

canDo: I can explain that something has come up, and put off a plan politely.
I can use everyday phrasal verbs like look into, sort out, fit in and let down.
I can choose between -ing and to after verbs like stop, remember and decide.
I can write a brief email with a clear subject line and three items.
I can follow up a phone call with an email.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. Who are the people? Do you think they get on well?
reading.talk: Who in the story let somebody down, and how did they sort it out? Have you ever fallen out with somebody and then made friends again? Write three or four sentences, or tell Wehel.

quiz.q: Sorry we're late. We were held ___ on the motorway.
quiz.why: hold up means make somebody late.

quiz.q: The trainer is ill, so the course has been ___ until next month.
quiz.why: put off means moved to a later time, and here there is a new date.

quiz.q: Have you finished ___ the report yet?
I clearly remember ___ the door, so how did it open?
quiz.why: remember + -ing: you did it, and you have the memory.

quiz.q: The new laptop has arrived. Can you set ___ for me?
quiz.why: With it, the small word goes last: set it up.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to end a work email?
quiz.why: Kind regards is a friendly, polite way to end a work email.

quiz.q: The meeting is at a bad time for me. Could we ___ it?
quiz.why: reschedule means change the time or date of a plan.

quiz.q: “Please call me back.” She asked me ___ her back.
quiz.why: A request is asked + person + to: she asked me to call her back.

quiz.q: In my last job, I was responsible ___ the office budget.
___ the flat is small, it's very close to my work.
quiz.why: Although joins two ideas in one sentence and can start it.

liveClass: Day 1: practise Lena and Samir's phone call in pairs, then change the problem: a sick trainer, a late delivery, a room that is double-booked.

Day 2: -ing or to. Each learner says one thing they enjoy doing, one thing they have decided to do and one thing they have stopped doing. Then pairs test each other: put it off, set it up, sort it out, look into it.
Day 3: the phone call. You are Carlos, the supplier. Each learner puts the meeting off and agrees a new time, then reads their follow-up email aloud.
Day 4: talk about the book: who gets on, who falls out, and how they sort it out. Then two learners read their three-item emails, and the class checks the subject lines.
